t: The Uneven Distribution of Fulfillment
x: The future is unevenly distributed. pic.twitter.com/ww6WTozUes — Paul Graham (@paulg) March 20, 2025 On first glance, this post would have you amazed at how far ‘ahead’ the US Air Force was, and that’s not wrong. However, although society generally pushes forward, individuals seems to travel the opposite direction. levels in tech: -junior eng -mid level eng -senior eng -staff eng -senior staff eng -principal eng -farmer — Kevin Naughton Jr. (@KevinNaughtonJr) February 13, 2025 There is a somewhat natural inclination for individuals to pull away from the “future” as they develop the means to (it is mostly a privileged endeavor). When I talk to my peers, it seems pretty unanimous that managing a plot of land in a rural area is one of the most attractive versions of their future. So, yes, the future is evenly distributed, but it’s unclear which side has the edge.

t: [Reading] Energy and Civilization: A History, Vaclav Smil
x: I picked up this book in preparation for a meeting with one of the largest utility providers in the country (and a customer of ours) thinking that it would give me a better backdrop on their business. However, I failed to put together that the company was founded in 1989 and 98% of this book is about energy in its fundamental sense; not in the context of today’s (or even the last century’s) corporate landscape. If the book was about what I though it was about, I may not have made it through. But the fact that the book was chronologically detailing the different inflection points of return on energy since the dawn of mankind, I had in my hand something I would have never otherwise sought out. So I had to keep going… A few things that stuck… The transition to coal (from wood) seems to me to be the biggest leap in “prime movers” based on the relative non-obviousness of use. Perhaps I’m the only person stuck fathoming why someone would think to seek out coal (buried underground) instead of continuing to optimize the other prime movers (waterwheels, windmills, etc). Perhaps this is the earliest example of the innovators dilemma? It didn’t occur to me the order of magnitude bigger than Hiroshima/Nagasaki the tsar bomba was. Interestingly, a short video of the bomb dropping was declassified by Russia in 2020, a few years before their large scale invasion of Ukraine. The term “fossil fuels” simply means that it comes from underground. For some reason, I thought there was a much more complex definition of “fossil fuels”, but alas, now I know. In 1954, Lewis Strauss (chairman of the US Atomic Energy Commission) stated “ It is not too much to expect that our children will enjoy in their homes electrical energy too cheap to meter ,–will know of great periodic regional famines in the world only as matters of history,–will travel effortlessly over the seas and under them and through the air with a minimum of danger and at great speeds,–and will experience a lifespan far longer than ours, as disease yields and man comes to understand what causes him to age. This is the forecast for an age of peace.” It appears he got everything right except for the cost of energy, which apparently, has less to do with the forecasting the potential of nuclear and more to do with wrongly forecasting regulation .

t: Building Slowly
x: This not ideal, by the way. Building fast is the de facto ethos of the technology world (and for good reason). When building software, the only excuse for slowness is lethargy or a lack of urgency; both unacceptable. The feedback loop (whether it’s internal or external) is the specific thing I (and other operators) “work on”. Signal in competence or customer value needs to be delivered to the person who can do something about it and the better you can orchestrate this, the faster value is delivered and accrued. Recently, however, in building a physical product in my spare time, my notion of pace has been shaken. PrintStack turns my online feeds (Substack, RSS, Research Papers, etc) into a print journal delivered to me regularly. It requires some software of course, but the end product is the physical journal where I can engage with the content without distraction; just me and the words on the paper. Getting the software up an running felt fast. The limiting factor was my free time and, thanks to Cursor and a few other tools, a production app that could generate a print-ready pdf out of my feeds was up in no time. But then it came time to print . I do not, as I assume is the case for most people, have a printing press at home. So once the PDF looked good enough, it was about 2 longs weeks before I received my first test press. Once I had it in my hands could I feel the product and notice many things that I didn’t notice when looking at the PDF online; the font was too large, hyperlinked text was styled as if I could click on it, spacing between titles of articles and the content was funky, etc. It then occurred to me, “was every product iteration cycle going to have two-week waiting period within?”. This is not my first time building a physical product. Years ago, my co-founder and I build a charging station powered by solar panels that could be dropped in anywhere (as long as there was sun). Although it was hardware (and yes, we had to wait for panels, batteries, inverters, etc to come from China), the feedback loop felt quicker because we were actually putting the hardware together, component by component. We could see the solar charging station come to life in front of our eyes. We continued building the frame and iterating on the design, reserving space for components that were still in transit. Because we had their exact specifications, we could build as though they were already present — invisible placeholders, but accounted for. When it comes to PrintStack, I will not get to see the product (or even a copy of it) before it gets shipped to the customer. In software, rigorous testing (and an industry which works on this problem) is abound and the exact product the customer interacts with has had hundreds of hours of internal testing, beta-releases, etc. In hardware, prototypes are built and pushed to their limits until production begins to hum creating exact copies of the prototype that has passed the test. For PrintStack, however, the words on the page (which follows the file sent to the printer) is 1 of 1. I never realized how much noise is on a webpage until I started removing it myself — stripping away layers to get to the words and images underneath. I'm not the first to have this insight ( Reader View got there long before me), but it took doing it myself to really appreciate it. I’ve spent the last few months doing exactly that. I’m sure there’s a faster way (piggybacking on Reader View libraries out there) to clean html content for print, but this is a rare opportunity I get to build slowly so I’m happy doing it the hard way.

t: [Reading] Under the Loving Care of the Fatherly Leader: North Korea and the Kim Dynasty, Bradley K. Martin
x: Did you know that Kim Jong-il’s first son, Kim Jong-nam, was assassinated by women who (allegedly) took orders from Kim Jong-un!? The book was published in 2004, before this happened, but towards the end, the author makes a few predictions as to who would take the reigns from Kim Jong-il next. Luckily, 20 years later, that info is available to us and I was surprised (although in hind sight, I shouldn’t have been) to find that the story of the N. Korean monarchy continues to twist and turn as history progresses. What is potentially less debatable is that this wasn’t the first time that a potential sibling rivalry (the stakes are high in N. Korea) played out. It turns out that Kim Jong-un’s father, Kim Jong-il, may have taken it upon himself to secure the his path to succession. As a 2004 Archive.org publication by Jerrold M Post of Cornell University recalls , Ko Yong-hwan, in his book Kim Jong Il as Seen by a Senior Official Who Defected, wrote about the accident in a similar manner: In the early summer of 1946, Kim Il Sung's sons, Yura and Shura, were playing together in the pond. Yura, who was a mischievous boy, had fun pouring water onto Shura and pulling his leg to topple him into water. Playing, they moved away from the edge of the pond, and when Shura, afraid of going into a deeper side, tried to come out, Yura caught him and stopped him from coming out. When the younger brother tried to move to a shallower spot, Yura pushed him into a deeper corner. The younger brother was at the point of drowning, uttering the sound of "blub-blub," but it was a funnier scene to Yura. But the old saying goes, "A tiger comes to a place where you find fauns." Thus, the younger brother drowned. If you forced me to defend the morality of Kim Il-sung and Kim Jong-il, I would have to take the angle that there’s a possibility they actually did not know of the conditions in the camps. The concept (and practice) of bad news being kept from the boss is an unfortunate reality not only in N. Korea, but in everyday business. So it wouldn’t take a stretch of the imagination to understand that the lieutenants to the Kims probably did not want to risk their lives providing bad news (that the economic landscape of the country is in deep shit) to the Supreme Leader. So, there is indeed a possibility the Kim Jong-il didn’t grasp the full extent…but rest assured, I have no interest in his further defense. This book is, as many other history books are, more proof that history is weirder (and more entertaining, to me) than fiction.

t: Improper Calculations for Improper Payments, etc
x: I was listening to conversation between Patrick McKenzie and Dave Guarino the other day and stumbled upon a calculation flaw I can relate to. Patrick McKenzie : Another thing you’ve mentioned to me before is the way formal accounting standards work in these systems. For example, if society establishes a set of rules and we accidentally overpay someone—let’s say $200 more than they were eligible for—we take a $200 hit to our score. If we underpay someone by $50 of the $200 they were eligible for, we take a $50 hit to our score. But if society establishes a set of rules, and someone is eligible but never completes the application process, we take no hit—because we don’t measure that number. Exactly. This falls under an area of federal policy called improper payments , and it’s one of my two pet issues. Like you just said, if someone applies and is denied inappropriately—or, even worse, can’t complete the application because it’s so full of friction—then really, we should view that as a $200 underpayment if they were eligible for $200 but got nothing. That should be considered just as bad as someone receiving $200 when they were eligible for zero. But under current improper payments methodology, which applies across all government benefits programs, we don’t measure that. This comes from federal statutes and regulations implemented by OMB. The way improper payments are defined excludes non-payments, which makes sense in one way. If you start with a universe of improper payments, you’re naturally excluding those who didn’t receive payments at all. But that subtle difference has huge consequences—we don’t count the people who didn’t get through the system. Patrick McKenzie : This is a wonky "legibility of the system to itself" kind of topic. I think a lot of people or advocates would hear this and say, "Oh, this is just the United States being stingy to poor people, film at 11." But it’s not simply that. If, due to a math error or similar, someone is paid $20 of the $200 they’re eligible for, that $180 difference would be surfaced in reports, counted as a mark against the program, and tracked over time across the beneficiary population. But the zeros—the people who don’t get through the application process at all—don’t get counted. This isn’t because someone comes into the office with the goal of dropping as many people off the welfare rolls as possible. It’s simply because we started with the mindset that improper payments are the problem to solve. So, we look at the universe of payments and zoom in on which of those are improper, rather than focusing on the bigger picture of access. Dave Guarino : Exactly. When you start from the flawed foundation that improper payments are the primary concern, it leads to absurd conclusions. Take it to the extreme: if a benefits program made zero improper payments because zero payments were made, you’d quickly realize something is seriously wrong. A benefits program is meant to distribute benefits. And you're right—there’s no one sitting in a room, smoking a cigar, and gleefully excluding 100% of underpayments from the improper payments methodology. But structurally, we just don’t account for it. This ties into the Seeing Like a State aspect of it. One of the reasons I've heard for this is that it’s a bit harder, bureaucratically and administratively, to determine what someone was eligible for if they didn’t complete the application process. Plus, it’s more difficult to get in contact with those individuals afterward. Don’t forget to count those unaccounted for. This is a fairly quick cross-check to any metric put forth. In my world, it manifested as an average, which necessitates a data point, and therefore ignores the scenarios in which no data was received. However, it was those that we were after in the first place.

t: Reality TV
x: My wife has always told me I need to watch more TV. Presumably, it’s to encourage me to turn my brain off. However, just the opposite actually happens. Why is it popular and what does it tell us about ourselves? I have no answers…just more questions. Could it be that getting a front row seat into other people’s problems helps us feel better about ours? Is there a version of ourselves that we see in the characters on screen whom we can live vicariously through? We talk about them as if we know them; is that a signal that our real-life social circle is small? Is that a good thing? In certain cases, I’m baffled that people actually behave like this. Or do they? These are the thoughts that cross my mind when Reality TV is in front of me. So…I’ll need to find another method of turning the brain off.

t: [Reading] The Crisis of The Early Italian Renaissance, Hans Baron
x: This book is out of my league, but I struggled through it anyway while in Italy. Although I feel like I only really grasped the content in a third of the chapters, it was enough to provoke thought and give me a sense of how advanced Florentine life in the 14th and 15th centuries actually was. It's an astonishing reminder of why the Renaissance has the reputation it does as one of the most important inflection points for humanity of all time. Here are a few quotes I highlighted… “In Conversino's eyes security, progress, and patronage are not found anywhere but under tyranny, and thus the final answer in the quest for the "preferable way of life" amounts to this: No true freedom can be found in this world, excepting the freedom of the man who, inspired by religious faith, renounces all things of this world, honors, possessions, and family. The only other way to what men may call "freedom" is a carefree country life in the midst of nature, dedicated to study and literary work, and this under the protection of a prince who sees to it that all men, assured of the stability of the public order, can follow their own pursuits, and that private, conflicting ambitions do not result in constant strife.” The problem is, when men take to the country for a carefree life of study and religious work, it's only a matter of time until humanistic opinions emerge. Then what? The Communist Party has learned that unless they are in complete control of the narrative, dissenting opinions will emerge. Even though tyrannical, I doubt that North Korea would encourage their citizens to move to the countryside and reflect, but I could be wrong. I'll report back as my next book is Under the Loving Care of the Fatherly Leader: North Korea and the Kim Dynasty . The debate between a quiet country life and an involved public one is new to me. I figure that nowadays, this is merely a matter of taste, but apparently not always so? On one side of the debate, a quiet life in the country is esteemed, likely promoting self-reflection. On the other side, however, progress (overall) may suffer as a result. I believe that the selection effect in today's world takes care of the dispute; if you desire to live a quiet life, you're better off not involved in politics (and vice versa). “Family, Church, Empire: each of them of is ruled by one head; consequently, past and present experience of the greater efficiency of tyranny only confirms what has to be expected” If “efficiency” is the end goal, I see no fault with the above statement. Obviously, the question is, to what extend is efficiency to be optimized? I see that men like to be busy; it’s an innate part of us. If we are not busy fighting amongst ourselves for the best possible government, we will fighting with others to expand it. We can’t sit still. Then, the tradeoff becomes a bit more apparent in my eyes; external or internal “fighting” ?

t: [Reading] The Psychology of Human Misjudgment, Charles T. Munger
x: It’s been a long time since originally reading Poor Charlie’s Almanac , so I picked up a pamphlet (called The Psychology of Human Misjudgment) at a Stripe Press event instead, as a quick way to get in the mind of Charlie Munger. It was not as quick as I hoped for, but I did feel I got a glimpse into his mind. I don’t think you need to read the entire talk to grasp the essence. Here’s Perplexity’s summary of each rule: Reward and Punishment Superresponse Tendency: We tend to work towards rewards and avoid punishments. We are highly influenced by incentives and disincentives, which can lead to biased behavior[2]. Liking/Loving Tendency: We tend to like and love things associated with what we already like or love, often ignoring faults in the object of our affection[2]. Disliking/Hating Tendency: We tend to dislike or hate things associated with what we already dislike or hate, often ignoring positive attributes[2]. Doubt-Avoidance Tendency: We tend to quickly remove doubt by reaching a conclusion, which can lead to hasty and poor decisions[2]. Inconsistency-Avoidance Tendency: We tend to be consistent with our past actions and beliefs, even when it's not in our best interest[2]. Curiosity Tendency: We tend to be curious about things we don't understand, which can lead to both positive and negative outcomes[2]. Kantian Fairness Tendency: We tend to expect fairness in all aspects of life, which can lead to disappointment and irrational behavior[2]. Envy/Jealousy Tendency: We tend to feel envious of others' possessions or achievements, which can lead to destructive behavior[2]. Reciprocation Tendency: We tend to reciprocate both favors and slights, which can be exploited by others[2]. Influence-from-Mere-Association Tendency: We tend to be influenced by mere associations, even when they're not logically relevant[2]. Simple, Pain-Avoiding Psychological Denial: We tend to deny or ignore painful truths, which can lead to poor decision-making[2]. Excessive Self-Regard Tendency: We tend to overestimate our own abilities and underestimate our faults[2]. Overoptimism Tendency: We tend to be overly optimistic about outcomes, which can lead to taking unnecessary risks[2]. Deprival-Superreaction Tendency: We tend to strongly react to the loss of something, often more than we value gaining it[2]. Social-Proof Tendency: We tend to follow the actions and beliefs of others, especially in ambiguous situations[2]. Contrast-Misreaction Tendency: We tend to overreact to contrasts and fail to notice small, gradual changes[3]. Stress-Influence Tendency: We tend to make poor decisions under stress[3]. Availability-Misweighing Tendency: We tend to overvalue easily available information and undervalue less accessible information[5]. Use-It-or-Lose-It Tendency: We tend to lose skills when we don't use them regularly[5]. Drug-Misinfluence Tendency: We tend to make irrational decisions when under the influence of drugs[5]. Senescence-Misinfluence Tendency: We tend to lose cognitive ability as we age[5]. Authority-Misinfluence Tendency: We tend to follow authority figures, even when they're wrong[5]. Twaddle Tendency: We tend to engage in pointless talk or action, often to appear knowledgeable[5]. Reason-Respecting Tendency: We tend to respond positively to explanations, even if they're not entirely valid[5]. Lollapalooza Tendency: This refers to the combination of multiple psychological tendencies acting together, often leading to extreme outcomes[2]. Understanding these tendencies can help in making better decisions and avoiding common psychological pitfalls. Citations: [1] https://fs.blog/great-talks/psychology-human-misjudgment/ [2] https://www.sloww.co/psychology-human-misjudgment-charlie-munger/ [3] https://novelinvestor.com/charlie-mungers-tendencies-of-human-misjudgment/ [4] https://jamesclear.com/great-speeches/psychology-of-human-misjudgment-by-charlie-munger [5] https://www.ricklindquist.com/notes/the-psychology-of-human-misjudgment-by-charlie-munger [6] https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/summary-psychology-human-misjudgment-charlie-munger-gilad-berenstein [7] https://aboitizeyes.aboitiz.com/post/a-summary-of-charlie-mungers-the-psychology-of-human-misjudgment [8] https://karthis.blog/psychology-of-human-misjudgement/

t: [Reading] Gulliver’s Travels, Jonathan Swift
x: I was first introduced to Jonathan Swift via the Conversations with Tyler podcast where he interviews an AI version of Jonathan Swift, who actually died in 1745. After appreciating the idea to bring him back to life, I figured I’d go read a bit of his work to see if I could form an opinion on how close I felt that Jonathan GPT Swift was to the actual Jonathan Swift. As much as I’d love to say that I could find the connection, that was indeed not the case, and as as result, I’ve added more Jonathan Swift books to my reading list — potentially, some day, I’ll be able to connect the dots between my perception of Jonathan Swift (through his writing) and Jonathan GPT Swift (in his podcast). Back to Gulliver’s Travels; a few brief notes… I don’t typically describe books as “fun”, however, I would here. It could be simply because of the ridiculous names like Brobdingnag, Glubbdubdrib and Houyhnhnms. Is there any etymology somewhere out there? Although I felt like a lost a grasp of the fictional world somewhere towards the end of Part III, I was still engaged in the adventures. I probably only captured 70% of the essence, but I even that is satisfactory (for now). In order to grasp 100%, I’ll have to read much more Swift and much more history. My favorite aspects of the book are the short summaries of the chapters before the chapter. For example, the book would read, *“The Author, being informed of a design to accuse him of high treason, makes his escape to Blefuscu - His reception there” ,* which is exactly what happens in the chapter that follows. It seems Swift has provided the reader spoiler alerts throughout, which I believe emphasizes the story writing, rather than the plot itself. Also, a fair lesson on brevity. Did you know that Daniel Boone’s favorite book was Gulliver’s Travels and he claims to actually have killed a Yahoo? In case you’re interesting in watching the full length 1939 movie rendition of the book, I’ve linked it below! https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rehNT9wIjUg

t: We’re Profitable. Now What?
x: For the past few years, nearly all growth-stage companies have been working to get profitable, with no exception to mine. Shifting the team’s mentality from grow-at-all-costs to “we all lose our jobs if we don’t get profitable” was a hard shift, but an easy decision (if you can call it one). After a few down-sizings, the meteor heading in our direction was in plain sight and we had to act quickly and there was no tip-toeing around strategy . Fast forward to today, we’ve clawed our way to breakeven (and a tad beyond) and although it feels like we’ve accomplished the impossible, nobody is quite satisfied. The obvious reason is that this financial milestone for the company translates to the individuals only inasmuch as we have employment; I can guarantee that the bar was a bit higher than that when first joining a growth stage company. So, the board’s official statement is now, “Great job. Now grow, but do it while profitable.”, which, to be fair, is sound advice. It tickles the mind to think that this statement essentially wipes out the value proposition for venture capital as whole, but that’s not for this reflection. The reality is that's exactly what we have to do in order for us, as individuals, to scratch our itch of ambition. It’s back to “growth” mode for us, but with an asterisk. As a company, we’ve done growth mode, we’ve done profitability mode, but we haven’t done growth-while-profitable mode. The clutch is currently down and ready for the gear to shift back towards growth, but there’s a psychological scar that’s keeping us from putting the pedal to the metal. It’ll be slightly new waters to navigate, but as with anything, adding some intentional (and largely financial) frameworks to operate within should allow us to shake that scare and get moving.

t: Optionality is Better Than Negotiation
x: In the business world (and the world in general), there's an emphasis on improving your negotiation skills. Books, courses, lectures, etc., all drive home the idea that negotiation is of the utmost importance; "In Business as in Life -- You Don't Get What You Deserve, You Get What You Negotiate" . If you've digested any of this, you've likely come across the concept of BATNA, which is the Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement. Knowing your BATNA is a crucial step to any successful negotiation, etc. However, I think more attention should be given to increasing the number of your alternatives, rather than simply focusing on negotiation. It should not be too hard to see, therefore, that if you increase your alternatives and give yourself optionality, negotiation will become obsolete, or at least less important. And likely, the outcomes will be better than those which were negotiated. A clear example would be in negotiating salary (which is the typical example in negotiation playbooks). The best negotiator in the world with one offer, will underperform a mediocre (or even poor) negotiator with 10 offers. This is simply a manifestation of the rules of competition (more options drive better outcomes) and a reminder to re-evaluate where you put your energy. Go spend it on collecting alternatives.

t: [Reading] World Without End, Ken Follet
x: Slightly more predictable than the first in the series ( The Pillars of the Earth ), and for that reason a bit less exciting, but a solid novel, by most accounts, nonetheless. Since I was reading the 48 Laws of Power simultaneously, it began to occur to me that nearly each law is demonstrated somehow in the story. Thus, is this Ken’s formula? Or for that matter, does every great novelist start with the laws of power and build around them? Here’s a few: Never Outshine the Master Early on in the book, the struggle between the apprentice, Merthin, and his master, Elfric eventually pushed Merthin out of Kingsbridge. Ultimately, this is for the better, but the relational strain between the two would come back to haunt Merthin over and over again. Although Merthin was the superior crafstman, this power law may have come in handy. Conceal Your Intentions Godwyn mastered this one, with the help of his mother, in order to rise to power in the church. Understanding how he maneuvered to power, mostly by not appearing to want it, provides a great window into the mechanisms at play here. Keep your hands clean Credit goes to Godwyn for this as well. Instead of doing the dirty work himself, he had Philemon do it for him. Stealing from the church, spying on others, etc was mostly the work of Godwyn, via Philemon. Use absence to increase strength and honor This law is akin to the saying, “You never know what you have until you lose it ”. When Merthin took off for Italy, he created a void in Kingsbridge and when he came back, his status had rose. Sure, he had amassed wealth while away, but it also became apparent to the rest of the townfolk that those in charge (ie Elfric) were not fit for duty. My absolute favorite part of reading historical fiction is being able to follow along certain characters and plot lines with records of history. Where the first novel ended with the assassination of Thomas Becket by King Henry II (a specific historical event I was able to draw the correlation to), World Without End didn’t seem to tie into anything specific, besides, maybe the plague? Next time I travel to England, I will certainly visit the Canterbury Cathedral, where Thomas Becket was killed. But how can I interact with a relic of the plague?

t: [Reading] The 48 Laws of Power, Robert Greene
x: Yikes… Not sure this is ideal model for how to live your life, but as with most things, it doesn’t hurt to understand them. I wonder the weights of each of these laws over time; what has been the most effective in this decade vs. 1,000 years ago? Do some become stale overtime? I’m sure there are countless book reports on the individual laws and how they’ve played out over time, so I won’t fancy that here, but did you know Robert Greene has a book with 50 Cent?

t: When Noise Is The Signal
x: Lots of fuss is made around distinguishing the noise from the signal and rightfully so. Noise can be incredibly distracting and can set your course in the wrong direction. But, in my experience, that doesn’t mean that noise is to be ignored. If you do, it can move around your org like a runaway train, and those who aren’t able to distinguish will suffer. What people observe (in other words, their context) matters a lot. Whether you like it or not, that includes both noise and signal, but in reality, mostly noise. What can not be directed, cannot be controlled. Over the past few years, as our org grew in size, we split our comms channels into function-based channels (like everyone does). However, as we’ve needed to downside, those various channels don’t serve the function they were intended to; surfacing comms to a select set of people responsible for those specific issues. So, I recently made a slightly controversial decision to direct all internal support-related communications (we have around 50 people) into one Slack channel. The obvious (and expected) downside of this was an increase in volume/flow though one channel, which can be hard to effectively manage. The upside was that I (and more importantly, the rest of the team) now have a beat on the noise and chatter that revolves around our operations. With that, we can begin to make strides on managing it. Without letting the noise flow in a controlled direction, it’ll naturally flow into pockets of the org, making it very difficult to manage. Fixate on the noise. If your job is to create an environment where progress can thrive, start by making sure you have a pulse on the noise. For only then can you effectively tease out the signal for the team.

t: [Reading] A Gentleman in Moscow, Amor Towles
x: Another Kindle read for me, which, in this case helped because I can sometimes procrastinate on large-ish books. However, this book kept on moving, which kept me reading. The video below from the author’s website does a much better job than I can portraying the vibe of the book. https://player.vimeo.com/video/183310610?h=37f98814bf The joys of reading historical fiction are bountiful here; particularly in getting to know more about the transfer(s) of power in post-revolution Russia, and also the Metropol Hotel itself where I learned my father in law has visited. Additionally, there could be something about single-setting stories that intrigues me. Where this book takes place almost entirely inside the hotel, one of my favorite movies, 12 Angry Men , takes place almost entirely in the jury room. Any more single-setting stories out there I can test this hypothesis on? A Questions from The Readers Guide Over the course of Book Two, why does the Count decide to throw himself from the roof of the Metropol? On the verge of doing so, why does the encounter with the old handyman lead him to change his plans? My point of view was not too nuanced on this question; the “purpose” of his life seemed to have evaporated for a brief moment. And the encounter with the old handyman may have helped the count reframe that very purpose, albeit unintentionally. It seems that “purpose” came fully back once Sofia came into his life.

t: Modernizing Age-Old Industries vs Modernizing Working With Them
x: All industries move forward (via technology), but some take longer than others. There are usually some good reasons why certain industries (healthcare, for example) shouldn’t be upended overnight; data privacy, lives at stake, etc., but there are also some needless ones. After working directly with century-old organizations for the past several years, I’ve picked up on a few patterns. It’s Not Whether or Not They Care; Rather What They Care About Throughout my first few interactions, and before I got to personally know the folks at the warranty companies we work with, I assumed they simply didn’t care . It turns out that it’s a bit more complicated than that, and I think I realize why. At a small startup, it’s fairly easy to make an impact (if you try). The lack of scale and red-tape allows any slightly motivated person to take an action against a particular problem, and many times, they can solve it. In an organization with tens of thousands of employees, that’s simply not the case (in general) so if you’re trying to inspire a single person (even someone fairly senior) to help you transform the industry, don’t misunderstand their lack of energy as a lack of interest. Getting Action So…what do they care about? Typically, as with anyone, they care about their boss’ perception of them and their paycheck. Many times, those two things go hand-in-hand. This is the oldest trick in the book, but worth restating: figure out how to everyone a bonus. Ignore your company’s mission for the time being and inherit theirs. Making Progress What can’t be measured, can’t be improved and if I had a dollar for each time one of our partners in warranty wanted to pull a report, but couldn’t… I’m coming to understand that this isn’t really just an old company issue, but true for most organizations who don’t make it a priority. I know of one company that’s been trying to implement NPS surveys for going on 2 years now, and still can’t figure it out. This phenomena of organizational inertia (or [extreme] lack thereof) can also be your problem to help solve. I started with data/reporting, but we shouldn’t limit ourselves to that. However, if you measure what your counterpart wants to (but can’t), you get the power to craft the narrative. And, as we all know, that is powerful. Meet Them Where They’re At? If we had it our way, our customers would do things differently; they’d all have an API, embrace automation, move quicker and have a higher appetite for risk. And then, the problem we’re solving wouldn’t exist. So be careful what you wish for and be more patient than your competitors as many times, it’s the last man standing (as opposed to the first mover) who takes the cheese. Displacement This is the uncomfortable part of innovating alongside old-industry folks. We’re all familiar with the “will AI/Software/Technology take my job?” question, but when you’re success relies on your counterpart or customer potentially being displaced, it gets tricky. What’s helped me here is make sure they see this displacement coming, and to help place them in a position to be on the right side of it, by being an active player in it. In Closing I love working with these people, primarily because it’s refreshing. The tech-world gets mundane quickly and getting a chance to slow down and understand what life is like in rural Iowa is a breath of fresh air in an otherwise fast-paced week. To borrow from Bill Walsh’s The Score Takes Care of Itself ; fixate on your inputs (how you work with your customers) and the outputs (modernizing an industry) will take care of itself.

t: Active Users
x: There have been numerous books and blogs written on how to think about who your active users are. Generally, the right answer is “it’s different for everyone and depends on the business”…which is really no answer at all. Recently, we've been refining our definition of what it means to be an active participant in our marketplace. There are (1) the individuals who transact regularly, (2) the individuals who state that they are open to transacting but aren't receiving enough demand to prove it, (3) the individuals who are behaving as if they are active (accepting jobs) but have informed us that they don't actually participate, and (4) any number of combinations of the above. I’ve found it helpful to pose the question; “If we meet 100% obtainment of this metric, is it possible the department/intiative fails? If so, we re-think. While at times a toiling exercise, the hunt for the appropriate metric can be sometimes as important as the performance against it. Where many back off and decide to use a standard ruler, I encourage the endless hunt for the right (perhaps complicated and clunky) metric. What can’t be measured, can’t be improved and a 1 degree delta (in direction) that seems negligible in the short run can have serious impact down the road.

t: [Reading] The Great Stagnation, Tyler Cowen
x: I felt like the book hit its stride halfway through. And by the time I was there, it was done (in a good way)! This is the third Tyler Cowen book I’ve read and, thanks in large part to his brevity, there will be more. Essentially, we (America) fell into a hole because “We thought we were richer than we were.” I think most of us can agree in both the truth and the harm of that. However, after reading the book, I feel like there’s something less- economistic , more human about America’s stagnation that I tried to put into words here . Another quote of note: “The more people trusted [Madoff], the easier it was for [him] to gain the trust of yet others. A small amount of initial trust snowballed into a larger amount of trust, yet most of that trust was based on very little firsthand information.” The gripe makes clear sense. However, are there downsides to the alternative; a world in which trust is completely objective? Do we really want that? What do we make of the saying, “The people crazy enough to change the world are often the ones that do?” Doesn’t that mean that although some bad things can happen when we trust blindly, progress as a whole would likely halt as well? Regardless of the unanswered questions I have, I wouldn’t think twice about recommending this book to my peers.

t: [Reading] Science: The Endless Frontier, Vannevar Bush
x: Loved the message, not the writing. Has he not read The Elements of Style ? Whole report/book can be found below: Science the Endless Frontier

t: Make it a “Multiple Choice”
x: I'm always surprised when I see decisions being made without a clear mapping of the options. At first glance, a question like "What should we do?" seems completely open-ended, with infinite options available. Urgent and desperate scenarios only make matters worse. However, if you start describing the outcomes of the first option that comes to mind, it will become clear that the number of feasible options is typically finite. Note that this is not supposed to be easy for every decision. Essentially, we're front-loading the "work" of decision-making into categorizing our options and playing out the consequences of each. It is through this process that the actual "making" of the decision becomes easier and clearer. This is probably what happens subconsciously anyway, but understanding the framework and being intentional about the process can encourage its success. I've found that this helps speed up the decision-making process, and if the options of each decision are documented (at least for larger decisions), it can help those around you understand the decision. I was once advised that being predictable is a positive signal for strong leadership. It means that those around you have successfully adopted your decision-making framework, among other things.

t: Laziness is the Father of Innovation, and the Grandfather of Complacency
x: What happens when all the innovation makes life good enough ? I'm not a professional (nor a pessimist) by any means, but why would any society continue to innovate past a certain level of comfort? Anecdotally, I've noticed that more of my peers today prefer to achieve just enough financial success that allows them freedom over their time. And most prefer to spend that time (like most of us do) in comfort with their families, loved ones, etc. Innovating is hard, and it seems that the incentive (a huge accumulation of wealth) is no longer as attractive. Apparently, the word on the street is that Europe is doomed. At one time, it was the center of the world. Now, are they the laziest of the bunch? give this trend another decade and europe is gna be feeling like a 3rd world country fading into irrelevance no gdp growth, no orbital rockets, no AGI we'll be exploring the solar system and they'll still be protesting retirement age in france pic.twitter.com/8e0gIk09qY — delian (@zebulgar) July 19, 2023 I plan to read The Great Stagnation by Tyler Cowen next, which may provide more color, but for now, I’ll be thinking about this a lot… Particularly, is this a bad thing? Are Europeans at all concerned? Or are they at peace with the world they live in? My assumption is that the Luxembourgers don’t have much FOMO at all. https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-vs-happiness?xScale=linear&time=earliest..2022

t: Facts Don’t Matter
x: This is not an original position. Luckily, I'm surrounded by some brilliant folks who've mentioned the notion; however, I feel it deserves a bit more credit. There's a certain fascination with facts. We have "fact-checkers" around election season, media companies are obsessed with "presenting the facts", and our justice system is focused on seeking truth, and so on and so forth. Typically, once we have the facts, we feel like we can make better decisions and judgments and live more informed lives. Don't get me wrong, facts and truth are important, however, they rarely end up mattering nearly as much as we give them credit for. In History The world is as we shape it. One of Ray Dalio’s observations in The Changing World Order was profound: both history and the future (all of mankind) is an average of the histories and futures of every individual who has walked the earth. Take the answer to the question: What will I do today? and multiply that by 27,375 (average number of days a person lives) . Then, take the person’s life and multiply it by 117 billion (the number of people that have walked the planet) . As a result, you have some explanation for the history of all mankind. In more manageable terms, we only have roads, for example, because some people believed they should exist and convinced others that they should play a part in building them. To the point - I believe that man landed on the moon. Some people don’t believe that. I have a set of reasons and justifications for why I believe that, just as other people have their own reasons and justifications for not believing that we’ve landed on the moon. The moon landing has inspired me to believe that other feats of mankind are possible and I try and turn that inspiration into what I do on a daily basis. My output can be explained (at least, in part) by the moon landing. At this point, does it matter whether or not we actually landed on the moon? In other words, what changes about what I do every day if the moon landing is faked? Likely, nothing. In Leadership I often share this bit of insight (that facts don’t really matter) with team members who are just joining. Typically, the reaction is surprise and then usually distaste. “Every argument should be based on its merits alone, decisions based on data and promotions based on value created”. Ideally, yes. However, there’s something that most of us, however objective we may strive to be, that seems to take that off tilt; human emotions. Persuasion usually ends up mattering more than facts. Facts are not very excitable, at least not on their own. Is this just politics ? Yes. It’s annoying and unfair, but if you embrace it, seek to understand it ( hierarchy analysis — Tyler Cowen ) then you almost certainly will not only navigate your company with more ease, but likely end up in a position to convince people to join in your mission. Leadership is not about just outlining facts — that would be too easy. It’s about forming a story that goes beyond the facts to inspire folks to join you. In Business The market has been paying for this unfortunate reality recently. Public Markets The market is speculative; you likely already know that. Typically what drives the market forward is what people believe will happen. Sometimes, this is based on “fact” (historical earnings to targets) and other times it’s based on particular beliefs about the future. I’d argue that without the latter, you can’t get to the former. Private Markets Fundraising from investors is probably more an art than a science. Reputation does matter of course, but why should investors care about reputation? Can they make money in the future on the value you created in the past? Not really. They use it as a data-point to better predict the future. Charismatic founders have a vision and get buy-in on that vision. They also convince investors that they’re the right folks to achieve that vision. While due-diligence is the “fact-finding” portion of the investment process, it’s typically not what drives the majority of the investment dollars in private markets. That can be attributed to the stories (not facts) that run through the business world. How to think about this moving forward? I once read a distinction drawn between “lying” about the past v. “lying” about the future. It turns out that “lying” about the future is technically impossible. This is a saving grace for overly ambitious founders, but it can still get you into trouble because although facts tend to matter less than stories, you will need to be keenly aware of the role they each play (ie. expectation setting). Don’t dismiss facts; just understand where they matter and where they don’t.

t: [Reading] Snow Falling on Cedars, David Guterson
x: While I read this one quickly (typically a sign of enjoyment), I left with my continued distaste for murder-mysteries. I’m not quite sure if it’s the predictability or something else, but I’m probably not recommending this one to anyone soon. It wasn’t bad , but I just didn’t find that it stands out in any way. However, the setting (assumedly the San Juan Islands) of the book reminded me of my fond appreciation for the region. The descriptions of the people, the buildings, the roads, etc matched my memory precisely.

t: The Good News is That There’s Bad News
x: Problems are the best thing to ever happen to us. Sometimes, in order to settle the initial nerves, I have to remind myself and others around me, that we’re likely not the only ones facing any given problem. After that, we begin an approach. In business, when we get a chance to solve a problem, we’re getting a chance to create value. If we execute on that chance, we have an opportunity to extract some of that value and that should be exciting. Without problems, or in other words “bad news”, what would we do all day?

t: More Info, More Focus
x: When you know what is on the other side of that door, you no longer need to wonder. If you’ve done the right thing and hired curious people, you should be aware that they will always wonder both why and how certain things work. This is a good thing, but sometimes, there’s a tendency in leadership to believe that information overload can stall people’s productivity, so the system becomes that of who needs to know. From my experience, this belief is typically the opposite of how things actually work. An Anecdote… A curious assembly worker’s job is to adhere paper labels to glass bottles. Lots happens before and after his particular station in the assembly line, but he’s particularly concerned with what happens after; he’s heard that all the bottles go through a rinsing process (both outside and inside) towards the end of the line. Since he cares about his work, thoughts of the paper labels, recently affixed to the glass bottles, getting wet and falling off during the rinsing process consumes his mind. As you can imagine, he begins to doubt whether or not the work he is doing is for nothing, becomes less focused, and ultimately less productive. That is, until he bumps into his colleague at lunch who happens to run the rinsing station. Over lunch, the rinsing station manager comments on the slight dip in how well the paper labels are being affixed to the bottles recently. To which our label-affixer says, “Don’t you have to re-do them anyways after the rinsing process?”. “No”, the rinser responds. “At our station, the machine generates a plastic cover for the label prior to rinsing to protect it! The rinsing process must come after the label-affixation in order to clear away any excess glue or residue from the other stations before mine”.

t: Conducting an Orchestra
x: 📖 Note: Everything below is simply a compilation of ideas from Ray Dalio , Steven Gambardella , and I’m sure plenty more, who express them more elegantly. Steven’s post also contains some video content showcasing the specific value of the conductor in the conductor-orchestra relationship. At times, it can be a struggle to find the right metaphor for explaining certain parallels. It’s occurred to me recently how much explaining power lies is metaphors (or similes, etc). The world is full of them and if you can connect the dots quickly, it can be really helpful, not only to the folks you’re communicating with, but to yourself as well. Recently, I’ve come across a particularly good one for explaining the skill-relationship between a manager/leader and their reports. In the past, I’ve had to maneuver debates between whether or not a manager of x must be kick-ass as x . Although there are plenty of folks who fall into the category of “yes, it’s necessary” , I tend to lean towards the other bucket. With anything, I’m sure the reality is “it depends on the situation and can vary case to case”, but in the spirit of resisting the answer-that-is-really-no-answer-at-all, I’d like to share a parallel that I found very helpful in explaining the argument that a manager/leader does not need to be kick-ass at x. Conductors understand the vision of the piece and direct the components to come together and execute beautifully. Note that they usually don’t create the vision; that’s the composer’s job. Although they understand the instruments in the orchestra, they’re certainly not the best at playing them. “ The conductor stands in front of the orchestra, with their back to the audience. They see, hear and feel the magic like nobody else can. What a privilege, what an honour.” - Steven Gamardella At the core of the argument for a manager needing to be kick-ass at x , likely lies the level of respect the team has for their manager. One way to gain the respect of folks is, of course, being the best at x . However, I think there are plenty of other ways to gain respect and check that box; one is being kick-ass at y (conducting).

t: [Reading] What Got You Here Won't Get You There, Marshall Goldsmith
x: I think I can summarize the message of this book succinctly; be a good person and don’t run your mouth. Below are a few small points that I remember taking away… The most helpful single line of advice is the question of “What should I stop doing?” Most advice is geared towards doing instead of not doing and it’s extremely helpful to inverse conventional advise at times. Believe it or not, this is the first genuinely funny book I’ve read in a while. Either my book selection sucks, my sense of humor sucks, or Marshall Goldsmith is pretty good at drawing out a few zingers in an otherwise serious book. I’m going with the last option :)

t: Outcomes vs. Levers
x: Outcomes are sometimes less important than the vehicle used to drive them. As many early marketplace operators likely know, the very beginning can feel like working for a staffing agency. Whatever the transaction is, you (as an individual) play a huge part in clearing it. One way of thinking about “scale” is to think about the levers you have on impacting the business. Lever 1: Conversations When you get an outcome (better performance, more availability, higher activity, etc) as a result of a conversation , it can feel great. Imagine you’ve noticed a business in your marketplace not performing well, and, since you’re in the early stages of running the business, you jump on a call with the business, provide some feedback and encouragement on how to find success in the marketplace, and as a result, they begin to perform. This is one way (Lever 1) of getting an outcome. Lever 2: Platform Using feedback loops within your marketplace to drive desired outcomes is another, better, approach. Now imagine that your conversation above revealed a key finding about the supply-side; they didn’t realize you were even tracking success metric A. Metric A, through your prior research, leads to more happy customers, so it’s not only very important, but you’ve found out that your supply-side can actually bend the curve pretty quickly; they have a high level of control over it (unlike many others). As a result, you’re now ready to build a feedback loop into the platform where all businesses on your supply-side receive impersonal communications when metric A is slipping alongside a drop in rank in your marketplace. This all seems very basic and obvious, right? 5-star ratings, reviews, etc in order to influence behavior have been around long before online marketplaces. The hard part is making the transition from Lever 1 to Lever 2 when the outcomes you get from Lever 1 are good! If it ain’t broken, don’t fix it, right? Not so fast. The value in Lever 1 is not the outcome, as it may seem when in the midst of it. The value is the insights you get through it. If those insights aren’t transformed into Lever 2, then Lever 1 is close to useless. I’ll go even further here (just to be controversial); the positive outcomes via Lever 1 actually have a negative impact on the business as a whole when you consider the cost to “undo” any outcomes down the road. In reality, needs of the business change over time and so do the priorities. For instance, if you’ve used Lever 1 to persuade businesses in your marketplace to prioritize quality above all else, what will happen when cost slides ahead of quality in priority? The undoing cost is high; you’ll need to re-use Lever 1 to change the habits of your supply-side (and we know how hard that can be). If Lever 2 is used, you can tweak the feedback loop, and game theory will do it’s thing! Can’t I use Lever 2 to undo outcomes via Lever 1? In short, no. Once your stakeholders understand there’s a human behind the curtain, things, in their mind, become negotiable or persuadable. Humans, after all, are subjective and emotional and if your carrots and sticks are delivered by humans, it’s very hard to change that mindset. My overall point here is not to avoid Lever 1 completely. My advise is to suss out Lever 1 loops in your business and work quickly to turn them into Lever 2. The longer you wait, the harder it will be to break through stages of scale.

t: Take the Stage
x: A friend of mine was given some advice from her mentor to take the stage. I (and she) thought that was great advice and I’ve shared it with a few of my team members so will share along here. Whether you know it or not, eyes are on you and typically, with that, judgements. Subconsciously, everyone is forming opinions about what they see every day. Luckily, we have pretty good control over what we individually do with our time and assuming that it’s great work, make sure you’re on stage when you’re doing it. If you don’t make decisions, arguments, etc, they will be made for you and you’ll be booted off the stage.

t: Baseball and Venture Investing
x: I had a conversation with one our investors about how their mental model has changed since they began investing. Much of the conversation touched on well-known ideas, however, there was something that seemed to contrast common thought; the ability to forget . “In order to be good at investing”, he said, “I have to forget as much I have to remember”. Learning from failures is widely accepted as a great way to learn. You make a mistake, analyze what went wrong and vow not to make the same mistake again. But in baseball, especially in pitching, this mindset can snowball into bad performance. Imagine you throw a fastball outside of the strike zone, a bit high. Then you say to yourself, that you’re going to lower the next pitch. The next pitch comes and it’s a bit too low and also outside. You focus on putting the ball a bit higher and a bit inside. Next one; it’s a strike, however, if you throw that same pitch again, the batter will smash it out of the park. So you try and locate the ball a bit closer to the edge of the strike zone, but the batter picks up on it and hits a double. “What went wrong?” you ask yourself. Now, you vow not to put the ball in that same location again (learn from failures). “I’m Crash Davis, your new catcher, and you just got lesson No. 1. Don’t think . It can only hurt the ballclub.” - from Bill Durham This sequence of events seems like any good optimization pattern, but in reality, you can quickly begin to treat every pitch as something you don’t want to repeat. As most pitchers know, in order to be elite, you have to be mentally willing to shake it off (forget) and throw that same pitch again. Why is this the case? I think it has something to do with a concept that Annie Duke laid out in her book, Thinking in Bets : people have a tendency to equate bad outcomes with bad decisions (and vice-versa), when in reality, there’s a great deal of chance involved in most scenarios. In her world, poker, only a fraction of the outcomes in a match are an actual result of the decisions you make during gameplay. The rest, is up to chance. If a bad outcome follows a good decision, learn how to separate the two. Back to investing… A failed investment will likely come with a few lessons: difficult space to conquer, market not ready, wrong founder-market fit, product is not a must-have, business model isn’t sustainable, etc. If you get carried away with “not trying to make the same mistake twice”, you may well miss out on good opportunities. From the perspective of at least one successful investor (and an awesome human), you have to be willing to repeat your mistakes as well as learn from them.

t: [Reading] Grant, Ron Chernow
x: Yikes, this book took my nearly 1 year to finish. Worth it? If for nothing more than a test of my endurance, yes, however, there’s more than I took away from it that that. As any good biography does well, I felt like I got to know Grant over the past year of reading this story. I won’t regurgitate my intake here, but will share a few nuggets that stuck with me. Grant was “near penniless” after his presidency and took a loan from Vanderbilt to stay afloat. It somehow doesn’t register with me that someone who we regard as one of the best military men of all time, and then one of the most powerful people in the world could fall into financial disaster. Entertainers and athletes, I understand. They have expensive appetite and are sometimes thrust into the spotlight prior to being ready, but Grant had no such appetites and plenty of brushes with the private sector. To his credit, most of his financial misgivings are attributed to bad luck and being taken advantage of. It seemed like there occurred another financial swindling by his inner circle every other chapter without relent; is there no way to learn? In retrospect, I’m sure I’m oversimplifying the ability to stray from financial swindling at that time. I image that with each event, the desperation rises. After a few consecutive steps into financial turmoil, the increased desperation makes it all the more likely a trap can grab you and the cycle continues. It does make me wonder, could this happen to any US President today (and in the future) ? - The ability(?) to not fear death seems more important a characteristic than any other in Grant’s rise. It’s hard to say if this is a good thing or not in my opinion, but clearly, his lack of hesitancy as a leader to expose himself in battle to gunfire gained him respect from his troops. With warfare presently not fought hand-to-hand in most cases, does this characteristic show any positives in today’s world? Is there an upside to not fear death nowadays? - I have never read two different biographies of the same person. It’s just now occurred to me what a fruitful exercise that might be. - I ended up visiting Delmonico’s a few weeks ago as a result of discovery from Grant. If it was good enough for him, it’s good enough for me (though he probably wasn’t too picky).

t: [Reading] Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, Gabrielle Zevin
x: Meta…very meta (I think). The highlight of this book for me was catching a reference to another book I read earlier this year, I Am a Strange Loop by Douglas Hofstadter. If my memory serves, it was playing on the idea that even is someone dies physically, they still lives on in our minds. The essence is captured well in this article from 2007; Opinion | A Partnership of Minds (Published 2007) The tie-in for Gabrielle Zevin’s story is - spoiler alert - for the young man, Max, who tragically dies near the end of the story. Another layer of the theme relies on the concept of “lives” as played by video game characters. In video games, characters get multiple lives and perhaps Zevin is arguing, by taking a note from I Am a Strange Loop, that this idea is not so far-fetched for the real world either. Aside from points-to-make, the story caught just enough of my attention to plow through it. Towards the beginning of the year, if you inquired about my interest level in a video-game fiction book, it would have been low. Now, I’m gaining a slightly better understanding for that world as a whole.

t: [Reading] Commons Stocks and Uncommon Profits and Other Writings, Philip A. Fisher
x: When starting this book, I was wondering how this possibly ended up on my list. I’m not an active investor, nor do I really want to be, however, I’m always seeking out knowledge. After about a chapter, it was an easy to put it together; I had seen somewhere the required reading list for new interns at Berkshire Hathaway. If you happen to pick up this book, you’ll probably say to yourself, “yea, this sounds like the words are coming from Buffet and Munger themselves”. One takeaway… The scuttlebutt method of gaining insights (talking to whomever you can in/around the company) on prospective companies to invest in seemed to me, at its surface, very inefficient. Fisher’s argument that the type of returns possible should clear any questioning of the time spent, which made sense to me, so I obliged to the point. Additionally, given the times (1950’s), the lack of information flow available allowed me to level-set. Then, I wondered about certain principle of picking a stock; information asymmetry. In today’s world, could the scuttlebutt method be of even higher value? Today, anywhere from 50% to 70% of trades are executed by computers. That means that any information published can be absorbed and is likely used by computers in their algorithmic trading; information asymmetry is gone, for the majority of trades these days. I don’t know if Philip is on to something here, but the scuttlebutt method of of choosing a great investment seems as though it may only get more valuable over time. Whether or not he knew that will stay a mystery, I suppose.

t: [Reading] Free: Coming of Age at the End of History, Lea Ypi
x: I’ve lately (and unintentionally) found myself reading books that take place around/in the communist revolution. I have no comment on that fact, but it’s made conversations with my in-laws, who left the USSR shortly after its Dissolution a lot more interesting. This book is good in my opinion, mainly, because it’s unclear of a particular point of view at first. I become ultimately skeptical, especially in non-fiction, when the narrative is too one-sided (even if I don’t agree with it) so for Lea to simply reflect on her experience was refreshing. In fact, it took some digging for me to figure out her complete take on communism. I haven’t read Marx, and am not for communism myself, but as any dutiful student of the world, it’s important to me that my exposure to different ideas is high. In all, if you’re looking for a delicate window into how someone who has apparently struggled through communism can turn out to be for the idea, this is a good place to start.

t: [Reading] The Last Lecture, Jeffrey Zaslow and Randy Pausch
x: I was gifted this book by some dear friends, the parents of my godson. It’s a short story that details the last lecture of a Carnegie Mellon professor, Randy Pausch, who was diagnosed with terminal pancreatic cancer leaving 2 young kids and his wife behind. Interestingly enough, the author of the other book I’m currently reading, I Am a Strange Loop by Douglas Hofstadter, lost his wife to cancer while their children were still young (5 and 2). After chatting briefly about it with my wife, we decided that I should end my streak of not needing to go to the doctor :) Some notes: Much of the book was centered around childhood dreams …not sure if I’m the only one who can’t remember what mine were? Should I be concerned about that? The notion that “brick walls” (or otherwise, life challenges) are there to test resilience is a helpful metaphor. Resilience is not a bad proxy for an input to success. Is Disneyland (even Disney) that great? I haven’t felt the “magic” yet, but maybe one day I will. What would happen if more people gave last lectures? Obituaries are typically written in third-person, but I wonder what a first-person obituary section would be like. Obviously, not everyone gets a heads up on their death as Randy did (he did mention being grateful for that), but for those who do, I’m curious of the themes that would emerge.

t: [Reading] Station Eleven, Emily St. John Mandel
x: Apparently, Kirsten Raymonde is a main character? This is likely a fault of my reading attention, but it didn’t become clear to me that Kirsten was even “a” main character until Tyler dies. It may not seem so (based on my above comment) but this was a page-turner for me. I was equally lost and engaged in the story, which is probably part of the allure; more gaps in the story for my mind to seek bridges for.

t: [Reading] I Am a Strange Loop, Douglas R. Hofstadter
x: Too technical for me at times, but probably the book I will gift folks over the holiday season.

t: [Reading] Dune, Frank Herbert
x: Many of my friends and acquaintances love science fiction. It’s almost like an elite club of book-lovers that I’ve always been curious about. And Dune, unfortunately, has still left me unconverted. Here’s, perhaps, a few thoughts I have around why that’s the case: Why do these stories need to take place in the backdrop of other planets during a time frame far in the future? The plot, the character development, the struggles are all stories that have existed in either true history or in present world. Perhaps I’m just missing the essence here? It’s too complicated. And I don’t see to value of the added complication. Stillsuits, the bene gesserit, House Harkonnen (among many others), Kwisatz Haderach, Sardaukar, etc…is all that really necessary? I was about halfway through the book when I found myself venting this particular frustration to a Dune-fan friend, he enlightened me; “Why don’t you just reference the appendix?” Because I was reading on a kindle, I hadn’t known there was an appendix. Kindles are actually great for term-lookups, but useless unless you know it’s there. Contrary to what it may seem, I actually didn’t dislike the book, overall. The story moved at a great pace and painted a good picture (I haven’t seen the movie) for my mind. When it comes to science fiction, perhaps, I still haven’t picked up the right one. But, I won’t quite give up yet.

t: [Reading] The Pillars of the Earth, Ken Follet
x: This book is longer than I thought. One of the disadvantages (or maybe advantages?) of reading on a Kindle is that I really have no idea how long the book is. Of course, there’s the progress bar that indicates how far along I am, but it’s not the measured mark of progress that’s present with a physical book. Anyways…long, but good in a subtle way in my opinion. As with any story, action ebbs and flows. The presumed “high points” contain battle scenes, political maneuvering, hunger, and other shocks, while the subtle moments are ramblings on architecture, masonry and things that progress slowly . I think part of the allure of this book to me is that the center of the story (the building of the cathedral) can sometimes hide as a side-story, but as the plot moves along, it becomes clear that it’s the center. And all of the “high points” are really just the supporting acts. Full disclosure, I haven’t yet finished they book so my thoughts may be somewhat half-baked, but I’ve read enough to have formed an opinion, not only about the book, but about the genre, historical fiction, as well. For some reason, with historical fiction, my mind tries harder to visualize the setting (characters, locations, major conflicts, etc). This is likely because, at least to some extent, it all existed , which allows me to cross-check some of the major aspects of the setting. Although imagination plays a major role in any reader’s experience, having historical relevance adds clarity to the picture for me, and thus, adds to the excitement. In line with being able to better visualize or imagine the setting, I’ve recently visited the UK and was able to pop out of London for 2 hour train ride to York. Thinking back, it would have been quite the experience to have started reading The Pillars of The Earth prior to the trip. The countryside, as a start, would take me immediately to William Hamleigh’s frequent long-distant raids. Additionally, it’s easy imagine Tom the Builder, Philip the Prior, etc roaming around the backdrop of what’s visible from the train as well (can’t help but to also think about Clarkson’s Farm ). And the cathedrals; well, of course it would have been nice to imagine the story behind each one. In closing, I read somewhere that this book was somewhat a departure — an 800 page one at that — from what Ken Follett usually writes. What if more people took the narrow path of interest? In this case, it ended up being the his most successful writing. I can’t help but to see this as a real world example of Robert Frost’s The Road Not Taken in which “[he] took the one less travelled by, and that has made all the difference.” Sounds like we should do more of that.

t: Politicians Should Get Paid More
x: I don’t necessarily mean that the current ones deserve a raise, however, the incentives to become a political leader in our country (and perhaps others too) are meek . It seems to me that the best and brightest are not turning to community/country leadership, but rather tech or finance. It's understood that the government functions very inefficiently, and thus, higher salaries for individuals who really can't do much seems egregious. Agreed. But, would our government function better if we had the best talent running it? Additionally, is a higher salary enough of an incentive to attract the best minds? A career in government is definitely a deterrent to most, but it probably depends on one's ability to make an impact. For good reason, our founding fathers inserted some friction into the process of being able to change things, but I think that friction has expanded over time to become immobilizing, thanks in part to market forces creating more attractive paths for brilliant people. Private and public companies are incentivized to create and capture value that’s ultimately returned to shareholders. In The Sovereign Individual , a question was posed to the reader that forced a thought around the value that the government creates for its stakeholders (otherwise known as citizens). Ages ago, the primary value of the government in the eyes of the citizens was to protect its physical well-being, generally, against raids by nearby groups of people. As the frequency of those wars and scuffles has declined substantially , I believe it’s important to incentivize our political leaders to think clearly about the value the government creates for it’s citizens today (and in the future), and, perhaps more importantly, execute on it.

t: [Reading] The Best Writing on Mathematics 2019, Mircea Pitici
x: I bought this book online during a Princeton University Press’s Flash Sale . I saw 70% advertised somewhere online and told myself that this is too good of an opportunity to miss out on…only to later find that this “sale” happens every single week. I felt that a book like this may be a bit too technical for me and I was, for the most part, right. However, even if I didn’t understand at a deep level the proofs, concepts, etc that the various authors of the various essays, put forth, I would at least grasp something. Here’s what I grasped: Mathematicians can disagree on mathematical concepts. I thought that math is fairly black and white, but it seems it’s a bit more malleable in some areas. Mathematicians can have a unique style. Similar to writers, fashionistas, photographers, etc, mathematicians too can be differentiated in their expression of concepts. Math falls more into the science spectrum of art v. science, but is not completely cut and dry. “Collection” books can be much easier to digest and I don’t read nearly enough of them. This dude, Mircea Pitici , has been putting together “The Best Writing on Mathematics” since 2010…another win for relentless consistency. It’s possible to learn about Mathematics, without learning Math itself. I don’t think I took away any technical skills or understanding, but that probably is not the point of this book.

t: [Reading] Where the Crawdads Sing, Delia Owens
x: I saw multiple people reading this one on the bus everyday, so I decided to pick it up. Not necessarily because I believed it would be good, but rather to better understand what the community around me believes is good. It turns out that people do love a good murder mystery.

t: [Reading] The Many Lives & Secret Sorrows of Josephine B., Sandra Gulland
x: This book was recommended to me by one of our investors, and also my first conscious foray into historical fiction. Apparently, this genre is much more popular than I previously realized, and as a result of curiously crosschecking facts, which makes me feel like an investigator, it has ended up being one of my favorite genres to read. In short, this is a depiction of events from the perspective of Josephine Bonaparte, starting as a young girl. Napoleon is not the focal point of this book; he only arrives in the later half. Perspective matters. In a similar vein to the saying “History is Always Written by The Victors”, it’s rare that we get a chance to view major historical events from a side lens. The French Revolution was complicated. I’m not a history buff, so maybe it’s just me here, but I left the book having more questions about the period of time than I did going into it. The book is by no means meant to be an account of the French Revolution, but it obviously is the driving force behind many outcomes. The last location I expected this book to be set in was on a beach . I’m oversimplifying it here, but only as the first few chapters moved along was I able to fully connect the dots.

t: [Reading] Working Backwards: Insights, Stories, and Secrets from Inside Amazon, Colin Bryar
x: This is one of those books I hesitated to pick up because I was under the impression it would be exactly like most books that profile a single successful business. While, sure, there was some of that, I found that the authors maintained an on-the-ground perspective (because they indeed were) which helped me move from the first chapter to the next. Here’s one particular note that stood out: “The best way to fail at inventing something is by making it somebody’s part-time job.” After sitting on this for a few days, I ended up beginning to re-organize my team. At that time, the divisions of labor were State lines. We had folks in Operations managing multiple aspects (customer service, dispatch, accounting, etc) of our marketplace for a single territory, each. While this made it easy to point the finger at someone for any particular transaction, I realized that nobody was able to focus on any single aspect of our marketplace, thus innovation fell flat. There was another byproduct of our former org structure (territory based) at the time: relationships. With the team managing all aspects of our Operations for a single territory, the one constant for our team were the supply-side stakeholders in their territory. Naturally, with the frequency of communication high, the team began to develop relationships with the technicians and those relationships were leveraged to get positive outcomes for transactions. However, that began to have downsides. Our leveraging-of-relationships began to hide gaps in the platform. Instead of fixing x, we were able to successfully train folks on how to get around x. Not a bad short-term option, but a ticking time bomb that I believed needed to be removed quickly. Over time, I’ve begun to have the point of view that some combination of vertical/horizontal organizational structure will probably be needed in the long run. Ultimately, I don’t think there’s a fundamental right and wrong for every business, but our decisions about org structure reveal the answer to the question; w hat kind of business do we want to build?
